title: What the AI boom is doing for Americans
gist: Noah Smith rebuts Paul Krugman's claim that AI is a technology 'of, by and for oligarchs', arguing the data center buildout is creating construction jobs and wage gains, generating large state/local tax windfalls, acting as a positive demand shock that offset Trump-era policy chaos, and delivering ~$172B/yr in US consumer surplus.

insights.claim: Construction employment has risen since the AI boom began in late 2022, both in levels and as a share of the workforce, contrary to Krugman's reading of flat nonresidential construction spending.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Labor data, not spending data, may be the better gauge of the buildout's real-economy footprint.
insights.quote: if we’re talking about construction jobs, we should look at employment levels, not spending
insights.locator: But I don’t think Krugman proves his case here

insights.claim: About 13% of the US construction workforce is undocumented, and Trump's 2025 deportations likely explain a pause in construction employment growth that year without reversing the overall rise.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Immigration enforcement is a binding labor-supply constraint on data center build schedules and costs.
insights.quote: 13% of the construction workforce is undocumented
insights.locator: And remember, this was at a time

insights.claim: Construction workers' wages have jumped relative to national average wages in 2026, which Smith reads as a sign of healthy labor demand rather than merely a composition effect from deporting low-paid workers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising trade wages signal tight specialized labor and upward cost pressure on AI capex projects.
insights.quote: there has been a big jump in construction workers’ wages relative to national average wages just this year
insights.locator: You might be tempted to think

insights.claim: Per Goldman Sachs data, the types of construction workers specifically required for data centers are seeing the biggest job gains.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Electrical and specialty trades are the bottleneck segment benefiting most from AI capex.
insights.locator: And it’s exactly the type of construction workers

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs estimates that 500,000 new construction and trades jobs will need to be added by 2030 to sustain the accelerating data center buildout.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Points to persistent trades labor scarcity and wage inflation through 2030.
insights.quote: Goldman estimates that 500,000 new construction and trades jobs will have to be added by 2030 in order to sustain it
insights.locator: And of course these are just the numbers so far

insights.claim: Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), cited by Krugman, shows only about a third of a data center's cost involves construction work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Most data center capex flows to equipment (chips, servers) rather than local construction labor.
insights.locator: He quotes Van Nieuwerburgh (2026)

insights.claim: Data centers pay property taxes, sales taxes, corporate taxes and fees that can produce large windfalls for state and local governments, funding roads, schools, transit and parks.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Local fiscal capture is a key lever in the political viability of data center siting.
insights.locator: Data centers can be a huge tax windfall

insights.claim: Loudoun County, Virginia, via early fiber access and fast-track zoning, became the world's data center hub and used the revenue to fund trophy schools, libraries and roads.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Loudoun is the template other jurisdictions will copy when negotiating with hyperscalers.
insights.quote: Loudoun has become a case study for the rest of the nation on how to make data centers pay off
insights.locator: Two decades into its experiment

insights.claim: Because data centers are hard to relocate once built, state and local governments can raise taxes and fees after construction, giving them substantial ongoing bargaining power over operators.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Hold-up risk: data center operators face rising post-construction tax burdens, a margin headwind.
insights.quote: they can even raise them after a data center is already up and running, so that relocation to avoid higher taxes becomes less attractive of an option
insights.locator: And crucially, state and local governments

insights.claim: Jared Bernstein proposes community benefit agreements requiring reduced electric and water rates for neighbors, funding for substations and roads, and investment in local public goods as a condition of data center approval.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Community benefit demands add to data center project costs and may become standard.
insights.quote: Such agreements should include reduced electric and water rates for the surrounding community
insights.locator: Here’s what Jared Bernstein suggests

themes.theme: AI capex as macro demand shock

insights.claim: The data center buildout acts as a positive aggregate demand shock that offset the negative shock from Trump's tariffs, deportations, deficits and record policy uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If AI capex slows, the hidden drag from policy chaos could surface quickly in growth and jobs.
insights.quote: just as Trump was trying his best to hit the American economy over the head with a stick, the AI boom came along and pushed in the opposite direction
insights.locator: But it didn’t, because just as Trump

insights.claim: Jason Furman noted that investment in information processing equipment and software was 4% of GDP but responsible for 92% of GDP growth in the first half of 2025, with GDP excluding it growing at a 0.1% annual rate.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: US growth is extremely concentrated in AI capex, creating single-sector macro risk.
insights.quote: But it was responsible for 92% of GDP growth in the first half of this year.
insights.locator: Investment in information processing equipment

insights.claim: Denying that the AI boom has a large demand effect requires heroic assumptions: very strong crowd-out, no demand impact from tariffs, and no role for corporate animal spirits.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The prior should be that AI capex is propping up the business cycle.
insights.quote: to believe that the AI boom isn’t having a big effect on aggregate demand would require some heroic assumptions
insights.locator: Now as I mentioned, it’s hard to know

insights.claim: Data center construction crowds out some other activity by absorbing scarce labor and by raising interest rates, making other projects harder to finance.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI capex keeps rates elevated, a headwind for rate-sensitive sectors like housing.
insights.locator: Data center construction certainly crowds out

insights.claim: Per Okun's Law, shaving 1 percentage point off growth would put almost a million Americans out of work, making the AI boom the main buffer for workers against policy-driven weakness.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A capex pullback would translate quickly into labor market damage.
insights.quote: According to Okun’s Law, shaving just 1 percentage point off of economic growth would throw almost a million Americans out of work.
insights.locator: According to Okun’s Law

insights.claim: By every measure Smith can find, AI has seen faster household adoption than any other consumer technology in recorded history.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Demand-side adoption supports continued usage growth for AI platforms.
insights.quote: AI has seen more rapid household adoption than any other consumer technology in recorded history
insights.locator: By every measure I can find

insights.claim: Brynjolfsson et al. estimated in April 2026 a US consumer surplus from AI of $172 billion per year, more than Anthropic's and OpenAI's combined run-rate revenue and about half of Nvidia's annual profits.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI labs capture only a fraction of the value they create, implying pricing power headroom.
insights.quote: estimate a total annual consumer surplus of $172 billion in the United States
insights.locator: How substantial? In April of this year

insights.claim: Medical advice and diagnosis has emerged as a particularly important consumer AI use case, and Americans in Pew polling say chatbots make them more productive, informed and creative.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Health is a high-value consumer AI vertical with disruption potential for healthcare incumbents.
insights.quote: Medical advice and diagnosis has emerged as a particularly important consumer use case
insights.locator: Medical advice and diagnosis

insights.claim: Despite heavy usage, Americans are overwhelmingly negative on AI, fearing job loss and, increasingly, existential risk, rather than resenting oligarchic capture of AI wealth.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Political backlash against AI is driven by safety and job fears, shaping which regulations become likely.
insights.quote: Anger at “oligarchs” monopolizing the wealth from AI doesn’t typically make the list
insights.locator: There are plenty of big problems with AI

insights.claim: Smith argues Krugman has a recurring blind spot on new technology, citing his 1998 prediction that the internet's economic impact would be no greater than the fax machine's.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Prominent skeptic narratives on AI value may repeat past misjudgments of general-purpose tech.
insights.quote: By 2005 or so, it will become clear that the Internet’s impact on the economy has been no greater than the fax machine’s.
insights.locator: In 1998 he famously wrote

insights.claim: Research such as Dolfen et al. (2023) and Barrero, Bloom and Davis (2021) finds large consumer and household gains from e-commerce and high-quality internet access.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that tech consumer surplus is large but under-measured.
insights.locator: Dolfen et al. (2023) estimate
